findings.title: Dropping signed coordinate extremes yields zero complexity for networks that realize arbitrary dichotomies
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2002__accepted__v3-bartlett02a-01 — Dropping signed coordinate extremes yields zero complexity for networks that realize arbitrary dichotomies
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 18, PDF pages 12–13 (printed 474–475); Lemma 19 and its proof, PDF pages 13–14 (printed 475–476). The absolute Gaussian-complexity definition is on PDF page 2 (printed 464), and the affected margin-risk application uses Theorem 7 on PDF page 4 (printed 466).

**Claim and assumptions.** Theorem 18 considers

\[
F=\left\{x\mapsto\sum_j w_j\sigma(v_j\cdot x):
\|w\|_1\le1,\quad\|v_j\|_1\le B\right\},
\]

where \(\sigma:\mathbb R\to[-1,1]\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(\sigma(0)=0\). It claims, for arbitrary sample vectors in \(\mathbb R^k\),

\[
\widehat G_n(F)\le
\frac{cLB\sqrt{\ln k}}{n}
\max_{r,s}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n(x_{ir}-x_{is})^2\right]^{1/2}.
\tag{1}
\]

The constant \(c\) is absolute. There is no input-norm restriction or coordinate-centering condition. The introductory description says activations are “typically” monotonic and smooth; monotonicity is not an extra theorem hypothesis. The counterexample below uses a monotonic activation.

**Error.** The extreme points of the signed \(\ell_1\) ball are \(\pm e_r\). The proof of Lemma 19 replaces their supremum by \(\max_r Z_r\), where \(Z_r=\sum_i g_i x_{ir}\), although the correct expression is \(\max_r|Z_r|\). The Gaussian comparison bound for the former quantity loses the common coordinate component entirely. When coordinate columns coincide, (1) is zero for every sample. The actual complexity need not vanish: already at one sample \(x=(1,1)\), the permitted activation \(\sigma(t)=\min(1,\max(0,t-1))\), \(B=2\), and outer weights \(\pm1\) produce values \(\pm1\). Consequently

\[
\widehat G_1(F)=2\mathbb E|g|=2\sqrt{2/\pi}>0,
\]

contradicting (1) for every possible \(c\).

**A reproducible false risk certificate.** The error can erase the complexity of a class that realizes arbitrarily many dichotomies, not only a singleton baseline. Fix any \(N\), use the same monotonic, 1-Lipschitz activation, set \(B=2\), and take

\[
x_\ell=(4^{\ell-1},4^{\ell-1}),\qquad \ell=1,\ldots,N.
\]

Define hidden units

\[
h_j(x)=\sigma\!\left(\frac{2x_1}{4^{j-1}}\right).
\]

Every hidden weight vector has \(\ell_1\) norm at most 2. At these inputs, direct substitution gives

\[
h_j(x_\ell)=\mathbf1\{\ell\ge j\}.
\]

For an arbitrary sign vector \(s\in\{-1,1\}^N\), let

\[
f_s(x)=\frac{1}{2N-1}\left[
 s_1h_1(x)+\sum_{j=2}^N(s_j-s_{j-1})h_j(x)
\right].
\]

Its outer weight norm satisfies

\[
\|w\|_1
=\frac{|s_1|+\sum_{j=2}^N|s_j-s_{j-1}|}{2N-1}
\le1,
\]

and the sum telescopes exactly:

\[
f_s(x_\ell)=\frac{s_\ell}{2N-1}.
\tag{2}
\]

Thus all \(2^N\) dichotomies occur with positive margin under fixed \(L=1\) and \(B=2\). All coordinate columns still coincide, so (1) asserts zero complexity. The support is finite; all functions and the sample-based selection below are measurable. If bounded inputs are desired, divide all inputs by \(4^{N-1}\) and increase the permitted \(B\) to \(2\cdot4^{N-1}\); the claimed right side remains zero.

Now set \(N=20\), let the distribution be uniform on these inputs with label \(+1\), and take an iid training sample of size \(n=5\). Choose \(s_\ell=+1\) exactly at support points observed in the sample, and \(-1\) elsewhere. By (2), the empirical ramp loss with margin parameter \(\gamma=1/39\) is zero. At most five support points were observed, so

\[
\Pr(Yf_s(X)\le0)\ge\frac{20-5}{20}=\frac34
\]

for **every training sample**, including samples with repetitions. Theorem 18 would give \(\widehat G_n(F)=G_n(F)=0\); Lemma 4 then gives \(R_n(F)=0\). Substituting this claimed complexity into Theorem 7 with \(\delta=1/2\) yields

\[
\Pr(Yf_s(X)\le0)
\le0+2\gamma^{-1}\cdot0+
\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2n}}
=\sqrt{\frac{\ln4}{10}}
\approx0.3723297411.
\]

The actual error is at least 0.75. The certificate fails with probability 1 although the allowed failure probability is 0.5. This refutes the application of the claimed complexity estimate; it does not refute Theorem 7 with the true complexity.

**Why this warrants rejection as written.** Data-dependent bounds for neural networks are one of the applications specifically advertised in the abstract. Here the proposed geometry estimate certifies zero complexity for networks that realize arbitrarily many dichotomies and yields a sharply false generalization guarantee. Replacing \(\max Z_r\) by \(\max|Z_r|\), or introducing signed coordinate columns, can preserve a generic logarithmic dependence on dimension, but restores an essential common-component term. Its omission has an unbounded effect: perturb the second column to \((1+\varepsilon)x_{i1}\). The same first-coordinate subnet remains available while (1) tends to zero with \(\varepsilon\). Therefore this is not a constant-factor discrepancy or a harmless exact-duplicate endpoint. The rejection consequence is confined to the advertised neural-network complexity/risk certificate; the paper's other principal methods survive this counterexample.

**Discovery and verification.** Compared the signed norm-ball extreme points with the rendered Gaussian-complexity definition and Lemma 19 proof. Derived the monotonic threshold network above, checked all 256 eight-point dichotomies, and checked all 21,700 distinct support subsets of size at most five on the twenty-point example. The calculation uses exact integer telescoping, not floating-point optimization. An auxiliary one-hidden-unit sine construction was also verified through exact rational base-eight phase intervals. All 20 pages and both appendices were reviewed after identifying the issue. Local constant, baseline and proof-detail defects are retained as screened notes rather than additional findings.

**Confidence: High.** The original theorem explicitly allows the chosen activation, signed weights and inputs. The zero claimed bound and exact positive-margin network construction do not depend on the unspecified constant. The probabilistic contradiction holds for every sample.

findings.title: Training-only sparse approximations do not cover maximum-margin ghost losses
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2002__accepted__v3-herbrich02a-01 — Training-only sparse approximations do not cover maximum-margin ghost losses
findings.markdown:
Paper: `2002__accepted__v3-herbrich02a`, Algorithmic Luckiness. Original PDF: an unpublished audit file.

Locations: Definitions 6–7, PDF pages 8–9 (printed 182–183); Theorem 8, PDF page 10 (184); Theorem 17, PDF page 18 (192), Equations (14)–(17). Theorem 17 is the principal application advertised in the abstract. This counterexample refutes its claimed omega-smallness and covering-number estimate. It does **not** independently refute a final high-probability risk inequality for the maximum-margin classifier.

For an ordered double sample \(z\in Z^{2m}\), Definition 6 includes in its lucky set all outputs \(A(\Pi_i(z)_{1:m})\) whose training-half luckiness is at least \(L(A,z_{1:m})\). Definition 7 requires, for every distribution and every \(\delta\in(0,1]\),

\[
P_{Z^{2m}}\!\left\{
N\!\left(\tau,L_l(H_A(L,Z)),\rho_1^Z\right)
>\omega\!\left(L(A,Z_{1:m}),l,m,\delta,\tau\right)
\right\}<\delta.
\]

Theorem 17 asserts that its \(L_{MM}\) is omega-small at \(\tau=1/(2m)\), with

\[
\omega(L_0,l,m,\delta,1/(2m))
=\left(\frac{2em}{-L_0}\right)^{-2L_0}.
\tag{1}
\]

This expression has no dependence on \(\delta\). Consequently the claimed property would force the covering inequality to hold almost surely for every distribution.

Let \(m=256\), \(K=384\), \(P=128\), \(\varepsilon=1/10\), and \(r=\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}\). Use orthonormal vectors \(e_0,e_1,\ldots,e_K\) in \(\mathbb R^{K+1}\). The feature map is the identity on the finite support. There are \(K\) easy examples

\[
x_i=\frac{y_i(e_0+\varepsilon e_i)}{r},
\qquad y_i=(-1)^i,
\quad i=1,\ldots,K,
\]

and \(P\) probe examples, all with label \(+1\),

\[
v_i=\frac{e_i-ae_0}{\sqrt{1+a^2}},
\qquad a=\frac{\varepsilon}{2m},
\quad i=1,\ldots,P.
\]

All feature vectors have norm one. The examples are distinct, labels of both signs occur, and all signs below are strict. The hypothesis space in Section 7 is homogeneous, \(h_w(x)=\langle x,w\rangle\), with no intercept.

The entire labeled support is strictly separable, so there is no infeasible training half hidden among the permutations. In fact,

\[
u=e_0+\frac{\varepsilon}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{P}e_i
\]

has signed inner products \( [1+(\varepsilon^2/m)\mathbf 1\{i\le P\}]/r>0 \) at every easy example and \(\varepsilon/[2m\sqrt{1+a^2}]>0\) at every probe. Consequently a maximum-margin direction exists for every permuted training half.

For any set \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,K\}\) of \(m\) easy examples, the unique unit maximum-margin direction is

\[
w_S=\frac{e_0+(\varepsilon/m)\sum_{i\in S}e_i}
 {\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2/m}}.
\tag{2}
\]

Indeed, for any unit vector \(w\),

\[
\min_{i\in S} y_i\langle x_i,w\rangle
\le\frac{1}{mr}\sum_{i\in S}(w_0+\varepsilon w_i)
\le\frac{\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2/m}}{r},
\]

by Cauchy–Schwarz. Equation (2) attains equality in both inequalities, proving optimality and uniqueness. Its normalized expansion has

\[
\alpha_i=\frac{y_i r}{m\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2/m}}
\quad(i\in S),\qquad
\|\alpha\|_1=\frac{r}{\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2/m}},
\qquad
\Gamma_S(w_S)=\frac{\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2/m}}{r}.
\tag{3}
\]

There is no representation ambiguity: the coordinate \(e_i\) forces each coefficient of an easy example individually.

If \(S\) contains both labels, two balls centered at \(\pm e_0/r\), radius \(\varepsilon/r\), cover its data, so \(\epsilon_2(S)\le\varepsilon/r\). An opposite-label pair has squared distance \((4+2\varepsilon^2)/r^2\), so

\[
\epsilon_1(S)^2\ge\frac{1+\varepsilon^2/2}{r^2}.
\]

For \(i=4\), the ratio in Theorem 17's criterion satisfies

\[
\frac{\epsilon_1(S)^2\|\alpha\|_1^2}{\Gamma_S(w_S)^2}
\ge\frac{(1+\varepsilon^2/2)(1+\varepsilon^2)}
 {(1+\varepsilon^2/m)^2}
=\frac{665223168}{655411201}>1.
\]

Thus \(i=4\) fails the criterion \(i\ge4(\epsilon_{i/4}\|\alpha\|_1/\Gamma)^2\). For \(i=8\), its right side is at most

\[
\frac{4\varepsilon^2(1+\varepsilon^2)}{(1+\varepsilon^2/m)^2}
=\frac{26476544}{655411201}<8.
\]

Hence the luckiness is exactly \(L_{MM}=-8\) for each such training set.

The full double sample contains all \(K+P=512=2m\) examples. Its first \(m\) entries are easy examples with both labels, fixing the threshold at \(-8\). For each subset \(T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,P\}\), construct an easy training set \(S_T\) by selecting exactly the probed easy indices in \(T\) and filling to size \(m\) from the \(K-P=m\) unprobed easy indices. At least \(m-P=128\) fillers are used; choose an alternating-label prefix so both signs occur. Every \(S_T\) is the first half of some permutation of the double sample and has luckiness exactly \(-8\). Thus all its learned outputs belong to the same lucky set.

Every easy example is classified correctly by every \(w_S\), since

\[
y_j\langle x_j,w_S\rangle
=\frac{1+(\varepsilon^2/m)\mathbf1\{j\in S\}}
 {r\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2/m}}>0.
\]

On a probe,

\[
\langle v_i,w_S\rangle
=\frac{(\varepsilon/m)\mathbf1\{i\in S\}-\varepsilon/(2m)}
 {\sqrt{1+a^2}\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2/m}},
\]

whose sign is positive exactly when \(i\in S\). Therefore the lucky set induces all \(2^{128}\) binary loss patterns on the probes, with zero losses at the easy examples.

The metric is average absolute difference over all \(2m\) examples. Even if arbitrary real-valued covering centers are permitted, an open ball at scale \(1/(2m)\) corresponds to an unnormalized \(\ell_1\) radius-one ball and contains at most two binary cube vertices: any three distinct vertices include a pair of Hamming distance at least two, while two points in that open ball have distance strictly less than two. Consequently

\[
N\!\left(1/(2m),L_{0-1}(H_{MM}(L,z)),\rho_1^z\right)
\ge2^{127}
>(192)^{16}
>(64e)^{16}.
\tag{4}
\]

Equation (1), at \(m=256,L_0=-8\), asserts the upper bound \((64e)^{16}\). Inequality (4) contradicts it by an exact finite calculation; \(e<3\) suffices for the integer comparison. For general sufficiently large multiples of four, the same construction has fixed luckiness \(-8\), exponentially many loss patterns and only a polynomial claimed bound. This is not a constant-factor discrepancy.

To make the failure an exact distributional contradiction to omega-smallness, let \(P_Z\) be uniform on the 512 labeled support points. The particular ordered double sample above has probability

\[
512^{-512}=2^{-4608}.
\]

At \(\delta=2^{-4609}\), the bad-cover event has probability at least twice \(\delta\), while (1) is unchanged. Thus Theorem 17's stated omega-smallness is false. The small value of this witness confidence level means the displayed final risk bound is vacuous there; no false nonvacuous risk certificate is asserted.

This failure removes the claimed useful complexity reduction in the stated application. A correct cover for this double sample needs \(d=\log_2 N\ge127=m/2-1\); substituted into Theorem 8, its complexity term is at least

\[
\frac{2}{m}\left(127+\log_2\frac4\delta\right)
\ge\frac{129}{128}>1
\qquad (0<\delta\le1).
\]

Thus the actual reachable-hypothesis covering cost is vacuous here, although the proposed fixed-luckiness estimate is polynomial. This comparison concerns the cover required on this double sample; it does not assert that every possible probabilistic repair must be vacuous, or that a particular final risk inequality has failed.

The proof error is the substitution of sparse vectors that preserve the labels of each training half for the learned maximum-margin vectors whose losses must be covered on the **entire double sample**. The ghost labels are uncontrolled by the training-margin approximation. In this example that uncontrolled variation is precisely the exponential probe cube.

 It verifies all 4096 probe patterns for a smaller instance, exact rational luckiness inequalities for the main instance, strict signs, both-label fillers, the integer cover comparison and an additional screened counterexample to Theorem 24.

Discovery method: traced the sparse-approximation proof of Theorem 17 back to the full-double-sample covering requirement, then designed training points with nearly identical label-adjusted directions and ghost probes that expose each selected support coordinate.

Verification method: exact maximum-margin derivation, rational entropy/luckiness bounds, exact integer cover comparison, finite distributional witness, exhaustive smaller-cube execution, and checks against the rendered original definitions and theorem. The independent parent reviewer also checked the original definitions and construction.

Confidence: high. The witness satisfies the original homogeneous algorithm, unit-vector and both-class assumptions; maximum-margin directions and coefficients are unique, all decisions are strict, the full support is separable, and the cover lower bound even allows arbitrary real-valued centers.

Reason for rejection: Theorem 17 is the paper's advertised new application exploiting margin, sparsity and clustering, and its essential covering claim is false by exponential versus polynomial growth at fixed luckiness. Training-label preservation cannot support the claimed reachable-loss complexity reduction. Repair requires a new control on ghost behavior or a materially different probabilistic application; correcting signs, constants or endpoint inequalities does not establish this theorem. The general framework and its other applications are not asserted false, and no separate false final high-probability risk inequality is claimed.

Every \(S_T\) is the first half of some permutation of the double sample and has luckiness exactly \(-8\). Thus all its learned outputs belong to the same lucky set.

Every easy example is classified correctly by every \(w_S\), since

\[ y_j\langle x_j,w_S\rangle =\frac{1+(\varepsilon^2/m)\mathbf1\{j\in S\}} {r\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2/m}}>0. \]

findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2002__accepted__v3-marchand02a__I01 — The central compression bound can certify a 49% true error as below 37% with near certainty
findings.markdown:
**Exact location:** PDF p. 12 (printed p. 734), Theorem 5 and its definitions of B(m) and δ(m); PDF p. 13 (printed p. 735), the first equality of Equation (3). The bound is subsequently used for reported certificates and model selection in PDF pp. 20–22, Tables 2–5.

**Claim and assumptions:** For independent, identically distributed training samples, BuildSCM with data-dependent metric balls and correctly classified compression points has true loss at most the stated U with probability at least 1 − δ. This is the main performance guarantee and the proposed basis for selecting p and s.

**Error:** Equation (3) conditions on the number of positive observations but multiplies by the binomial probability of that same count again. Correctly conditioned class-specific correctness probabilities do not support the displayed overall-loss bound.

**Exact reproducible violation:** Let X = {1, …, 100} × [0, 1], with the group uniform and the second coordinate continuously uniform. Groups 1–50 are positive and groups 51–100 negative. Use the metric that is 0 at identical points, 1 between distinct points in one group, and 2 between groups. This is a metric expressly permitted by Section 4. Set m = 10000, p = 1/(2m), s = 1, conjunction type, and radius offset ε = 0.1.

Let E be the event that every group occurs 40–180 times. A binomial Chernoff bound and union bound give P(E) ≥ 0.9999984651642804. On E, a P-centered ball with another P point in its own group as border predicts 1 exactly on that group and covers all negative observations. Its utility exceeds m_n − 0.5 ≥ 1999.5. Every admissible N-centered ball covers at most 180 negative observations; a P-centered ball including another group predicts 1 everywhere and has utility 0. Hence BuildSCM selects a ball for a largest positive group, containing a ∈ [40, 180] observations, and stops. Its positive center and distinct positive border are correctly classified and reconstruct the same ball, satisfying the theorem’s compression constraint.

This classifier has true error 49/100. Its parameters are c_p = b_p = 1, c_n = k_n = 0, and k_p = m_p − a. The claimed bound uses B = m_p(m_p − 1) choose(m_p − 2, a − 2) and denominator m_n + a − 2. For δ = 0.05, uniformly throughout E:

- ln B + ln(1/δ(m)) ≤ 940.1812982558216;
- m_n + a − 2 ≥ 2038;
- therefore U ≤ 1 − exp(−940.1812982558216/2038) = 0.3695525447587202 < 0.49.

Thus the supposed 95% guarantee fails with probability above 99.9998%. The complete inequality derivation and feature enumeration are in counterexample.md. This uniform probabilistic proof is independent of the following illustrations: equal counts of 100 per group give U = 0.0972253; 1000 seeded independent group-count samples all violate the bound, with U ranging from 0.10180 to 0.12448.

 The script also checks metric inequalities, every possible feature type, exact integer binomial arithmetic, and compression parameters.

**Why rejection is warranted:** The main distribution-free guarantee can certify a high-error classifier as accurate with near certainty. It supports the abstract’s performance and model-selection contribution, the central theory, and all bound-based certificates and selection in the experiments. Repair requires replacing the conditional class-count analysis and bound, rather than fixing a constant or deleting an optional example. The algorithm and observed sparsity may remain useful, but the central guarantee is false as written.

**Discovery and verification:** Independently traced Equation (3), built the algorithm-compatible counterexample, rechecked the original rendered definitions, Theorem 5, and Equation (3), and verified the exact event and inequalities. The parent reviewer independently rederived the construction and reran every assertion. A later primary paper coauthored by both original authors confirms exactly this proof error: Hussain et al., [Revised Loss Bounds for the Set Covering Machine and Sample-Compression Loss Bounds for Imbalanced Data](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume8/hussain07a/hussain07a.pdf), JMLR 8 (2007), Section 3, printed pp. 2536–2537. Its original PDF and rendered correction pages are saved with the evidence.

**Confidence: High.** This is an exact distribution-level contradiction satisfying all original algorithm and compression assumptions. Independent verification and primary-source confirmation agree.

findings.title: The claimed sampling impossibility ignores the dependence of the subgroup and global class probabilities
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2002__accepted__v3-scheffer02a-01 — The claimed sampling impossibility ignores the dependence of the subgroup and global class probabilities
findings.markdown:
**Exact locations.** Section 4.5 and Theorem 12, PDF page 17 / printed page 849; its proof and equations (81)–(82), PDF page 18 / printed page 850. The governing definition of `p0` is the first paragraph of PDF page 7 / printed page 839. The additive approximation problem is Definition 2, PDF page 3 / printed page 835, and Theorem 4, PDF page 6 / printed page 838. The impossibility is advertised in the abstract and introduction, PDF pages 1–2, and repeated as a guide to utility selection in Section 6, PDF page 21 / printed page 853.

**Claim and assumptions.** Theorem 12 says there is no algorithm satisfying Theorem 4 for

```text
f(h) = g/(1-g) (p-p0)^2.
```

Here `g` is the fraction of the database in a subgroup, `p` is the binary target probability within it, and `p0` is the target probability in the whole database. Thus `p0` is not an independently supplied control baseline. Theorem 4 asks for an additive `epsilon` approximation to the best `n` hypotheses, with probability at least `1-delta`. The hypothesis set is finite. Definition 3 permits an estimated utility with a valid confidence bound; it does not restrict algorithms to one particular plug-in estimator.

**Error.** If `q` is the target probability outside the subgroup, the law of total probability imposes

```text
p0 = g p + (1-g) q,
f(h) = g(1-g) (p-q)^2 <= 1/4.
```

The proof considers divergence of `g/(1-g)` while ignoring the corresponding shrinking of `p-p0`. Its assertion that this utility is unbounded is false on the defined problem domain. For example, take a database of `N` items, with `N-1` positive items all in the subgroup and one negative item outside. Then the coefficient is `N-1`, but the actual utility is `(N-1)/N^2`, tending to zero.

Boundedness alone would not establish estimability of every possible functional. The following construction gives the required algorithm and finite uniform sample bound.

Let the four joint probabilities of subgroup membership `B` and binary label `Y` be

```text
a = Pr(B=1,Y=1), b = Pr(B=1,Y=0),
c = Pr(B=0,Y=1), d = Pr(B=0,Y=0),
t = a+c = p0.
```

The exact same utility is

```text
F(a,b,c,d) = t(1-t) - ab/(a+b) - cd/(c+d).
```

Set terms `0/0` to zero. This is the continuous extension at empty or full subgroups. It equals total Bernoulli variance minus the expected within-group variance. Both variance terms have a variational representation as the minimum expected squared loss over predictions in `[0,1]`. Since these losses are bounded by one, each minimum is 1-Lipschitz in the L1 distance between the four cell probabilities. Therefore

```text
|F(P)-F(Q)| <= 2 ||P-Q||_1 <= 8 max_j |P_j-Q_j|.
```

Draw `m` database items independently with replacement. For every hypothesis, form the four empirical cell probabilities and evaluate this formula. A union bound over the four cells and all hypotheses, using Hoeffding, gives

```text
Pr(max_h |Fhat_h-F_h| > 8 sqrt(ln(8 |H|/delta)/(2m))) <= delta.
```

Consequently,

```text
m >= ceil(128 epsilon^(-2) ln(8 |H|/delta))
```

makes every score accurate to `epsilon/2` simultaneously with probability at least `1-delta`. Return the `n` highest empirical scores. For every excluded hypothesis `h` and returned hypothesis `r`,

```text
F(h) <= Fhat(h)+epsilon/2 <= Fhat(r)+epsilon/2 <= F(r)+epsilon.
```

This is exactly the guarantee Theorem 12 says no algorithm can satisfy. The bound is independent of database size. It applies to databases larger than the bound; smaller databases can be scanned exactly. This is not a counterargument that relies only on scanning the full database.

The estimator reestimates `p0` through the empirical label frequency. It estimates the same true utility even if the true global `p0` is supplied. Definition 3 allows this, and Theorem 12 rules out all algorithms. The singular behavior of a particular fixed-`p0` plug-in estimator cannot prove that no other estimator exists. Relative error near a zero utility is a separate question; Theorem 12 concerns the stated additive guarantee.

**Reproducible evidence and verification.** `checks.py` exhaustively checks the identities and the bound with exact rational arithmetic on all 5,456 contingency tables of size 30, including boundary tables; the maximum is exactly `1/4`. It also checks 40,000 pairs of probability vectors against the Lipschitz bound, and runs the constructive algorithm 100 times on a finite 20,000-item database with four hypotheses, using 18,459 queries per run. The analytic proof, rather than those runs, establishes the uniform guarantee. An independent second reviewer inspected those original pages and separately derived the same constructive bound.

**Why rejection is warranted.** The impossible-versus-estimable distinction is an explicit main contribution in the abstract, not an incidental proof step. Its conclusion is reversed for the stated popular utility family: sampling is possible with a distribution-free finite sample bound. Correcting it requires withdrawing the negative theorem and its recommendation about which utility functions admit sampling. This does not claim that the measured speedups for other utility families disappear.

**Discovery method:** traced the claimed singularity against the original subgroup probability definitions, then rewrote the utility as a four-cell variance functional. **Verification method:** independent symbolic construction of a valid confidence bound and top-`n` algorithm, exact rational enumeration, boundary examples, and independently reproduced numerical checks. **Confidence: high.** The counteralgorithm operates under the stated model and directly satisfies the supposedly impossible guarantee.

sections.html:
Let g be subgroup prevalence, p its positive-class frequency, and q the frequency outside it. The overall frequency is fixed by these quantities:

\[ p_0=gp+(1-g)q,\qquad f=\frac{g}{1-g}(p-p_0)^2=g(1-g)(p-q)^2\leq\frac14 \]

The audit estimates the four subgroup/class cell probabilities. A union bound gives a finite sample size sufficient for the advertised approximation, contradicting the impossibility claim.

findings.title: The generic algorithm can accumulate approximation error across accepted hypotheses
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2002__accepted__v3-scheffer02a-02 — The generic algorithm can accumulate approximation error across accepted hypotheses
findings.markdown:
**Exact locations.** Table 1, step 3(e)i, PDF page 5 / printed page 837; Theorem 4, PDF page 6 / printed page 838. Appendix A invariant `(I3)`, PDF page 22 / printed page 854; Case (1), “Show (I3),” PDF page 24 / printed page 856; final acceptance proof, PDF page 27 / printed page 859.

**Claim and assumptions.** The algorithm claims the additive `epsilon` guarantee of Theorem 4 for any estimated utilities with valid confidence bounds as defined in Definition 3. Unbiasedness is not required. A returned hypothesis can be accepted when its lower confidence bound is within `epsilon` of the largest upper bound outside the current empirical best set. The requested number of remaining outputs decreases after acceptance.

**Error and exact counterexample.** Approximate acceptances can protect the newly accepted hypothesis while leaving a previously accepted, worse hypothesis without the advertised guarantee. This occurs even when every common and hypothesis-specific confidence interval is correct deterministically at every sample size.

Use four hypotheses in order `g,c,d,a`, request `n=3`, and set `epsilon=1/10`, `delta=1/10`. Let each hypothesis have a constant per-item utility, so its exact empirical mean on every database and every iid query sequence is respectively

```text
f(g)=0, f(c)=9/100, f(d)=18/100, f(a)=27/100.
```

The estimated utility is that empirical mean plus a specified deterministic sample-size bias. The following table gives the estimates and the valid radii for the active hypotheses; each cell is `estimate ; radius`.

| Sample size | g | c | d | a |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | `0 ; .001` | `0 ; .091` | `.18 ; .301` | `.27 ; .301` |
| 2 | already output | `.09 ; .001` | `0 ; .181` | `.27 ; .301` |
| 3 | already output | already output | `.18 ; .001` | `0 ; .271` |

For sample sizes at least four, all biases are zero and every radius is `.001/(m-3)`. Use common radius `.301` through sample size three and `.001/(m-3)` thereafter. All bounds are strictly positive, nonincreasing in sample size, independent of the confidence argument, and vanish. Every estimation error is within its radius with probability one for every database, every sample size, and every query sequence. All true and estimated utilities are in `[0,1]`. Thus this is a valid instance of Definition 3, not a confidence-interval failure. The estimates are deliberately biased; the example does not assert failure of the natural plug-in estimators in Section 4.

The worst-case stopping parameter in step 2 is `M=4`. Through the first three iterations the common stopping radius exceeds `epsilon/2`. Process the full for-loop, recomputing the active set, remaining output count, and empirical best set after every acceptance:

1. At sample size 1, the best three are `a,d,g`, with ties placing `g` before `c`. For `g`, the acceptance right-hand side is `.001+.091-.1=-.008`, so it is output. Neither `d` nor `a` is accepted because their large valid radii block acceptance. No hypothesis is discarded.
2. At sample size 2, the best two are `a,c`. The acceptance right-hand side for `c` is `.001+.181-.1=.082`, below its estimate `.09`, so `c` is output. The others remain.
3. At sample size 3, `d` is best empirically. Its acceptance right-hand side is `.001+.271-.1=.172`, below `.18`, so `d` is output and the requested output count reaches zero.

The final output is `{g,c,d}`, excluding `a`. The excluded utility exceeds the minimum returned utility by `.27`, although the requested tolerance is `.1`. The failure probability is one while every confidence event holds. The trace uses a coherent, charitable interpretation of the paper’s inconsistent `H_i/H_(i+1)` and `n_i/n_(i+1)` indexing. It executes the entire same-sample for-loop; it does not rely on the proof’s one-action-per-iteration simplification.

**Where the proof fails.** After accepting a hypothesis, the invariant for previously output hypotheses becomes stronger because `n_i` decreases. The Case (1) proof checks `(I3)` for the newly accepted hypothesis only. It does not establish the strengthened invariant for old outputs. A later approximate acceptance can leave a better hypothesis behind, as the trace shows.

The loss is not bounded by a universal constant multiple of the requested tolerance. `gss-family.py` constructs the same phenomenon for any requested `n>=2`: use `n+1` constant utility targets `v_j=.9 j epsilon`, with `epsilon=1/(2n)`, and successively suppress one next hypothesis’s estimate while retaining valid radii. The algorithm returns `h_0,...,h_(n-1)`, excluding `h_n`; its error is `.9 n epsilon`. All utilities remain at most `.45`, and all confidence events hold with probability one. Exact rational executions for `n=2,...,50` confirm this family. At `n=50`, the requested tolerance is `.01` and the actual gap is `.45`.

**Reproducible evidence and verification.** Run gss-counterexample.py for the complete exact rational four-hypothesis trace; its JSON result records every acceptance, discard test, best set, and threshold. Run gss-family.py for the unbounded-in-`n` family; results are in gss-family.json. Original Table 1 and the faulty invariant step are rendered as an unpublished page image and an unpublished page image. An independent reviewer reran the four-hypothesis script and inspected those original pages and Definition 3.

**Why rejection is warranted.** Theorem 4 is the central guarantee of the generic algorithm. This example satisfies the explicit confidence-bound assumptions yet violates that guarantee with certainty. A correction must change acceptance or approximation budgeting, impose substantive additional estimator restrictions, and supply a new invariant/proof. For example, reserving approximation for final selection changes the early acceptance rule; dividing tolerance across stages changes the dependence of sample requirements on `n`. The existing empirical speedup claims do not establish the behavior of such a revised algorithm. This is not a transcription error or a fixed missing constant. Its demonstrated scope is the advertised generic theorem, not a claimed rerun failure of the original subgroup implementation.

**Discovery method:** traced the quantified loop invariant when the remaining output count decreases and constructed successive acceptances that undermine an earlier output. **Verification method:** exact rational execution of the full algorithm with confidence events true for every sequence, plus a parameterized family and independent reproduction. **Confidence: high.** The only nonstandard feature is the explicitly disclosed deterministic bias, which the stated generic assumptions permit.

Other observations were screened separately, including the fourth-root versus `epsilon^-2` sample-bound arithmetic, finite-sample failure of empirical-normal confidence intervals, adaptive use of confidence levels, and local equation slips. Original source code, the proprietary juice database, split seeds, and raw experimental runs were not recovered. No missing code, failed rerun, or unmeasured reversal of Figure 1 or Figure 2 is asserted as a finding.

sections.html:
For n = 3 and ε = 0.1, the audit gives four true utilities 0, 0.09, 0.18, and 0.27. Every supplied confidence interval is valid, but successive rounds accept the first three and exclude the best.

\[ \text{best excluded utility}-\text{worst returned utility}=0.27>0.1 \]

This happens deterministically. In a larger construction, the gap grows as 0.9nε.
